questions.stitle: Scenario 1 - National rail operator, ticketing merger
questions.scenario: You consult to the Chief Architect of a national passenger rail operator that has just absorbed a regional franchise. The operator has a mature EA practice using the TOGAF Standard, and the CIO sponsors the EA program. An EA project has been initiated to integrate the franchise's ticketing and scheduling systems; the scope is agreed. The Chief Architect explains that two previous franchise integrations stalled because station managers and the regional operations staff were never brought into the process, and their local knowledge was lost. The Chief Architect insists this integration must engage the right people from both organizations from the outset.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend an approach that develops an architecture addressing the Chief Architect's concern. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You develop a Communications Plan aimed at the regional franchise's station managers and operations staff so they are made aware of the architecture and can comment on it as work proceeds.
o.B: You identify the key stakeholders across both the national operator and the regional franchise, classify their position and influence in a Stakeholder Map, select the most relevant viewpoints for each, validate that their concerns are addressed, and communicate with them early and frequently so they understand the architecture process.
o.C: You run business scenarios with the affected operations staff to determine who will support or block the integration, derive the requirements the architecture must satisfy, and identify the most relevant viewpoints validated with those staff.
o.D: You run a Phase A pilot integration at two stations to prove the preferred supplier's ticketing platform, map it to a viewpoint library, and once operations staff confirm it meets their needs, issue an Architecture Contract to the supplier.

rat.A: Third (1). The Communications Plan is produced from stakeholder analysis, not instead of it; scoping it to the franchise only omits key national-operator stakeholders and reduces engagement to one-way awareness.
rat.B: Best (5). Stakeholder analysis and a Stakeholder Map is the Phase A technique TOGAF recommends (G186); it is a major output feeding other Phase A products, covers both organizations, and drives active early and frequent engagement of the key people the concern is about.
rat.C: Second (3). Business scenarios engage stakeholders and derive requirements, but this omits the Stakeholder Map and the explicit identification and classification of the key players by position and influence.
rat.D: Distractor (0). TOGAF does not recommend Phase A pilots to prove supplier feasibility, and this misuses the Statement of Architecture Work and Architecture Contract sequence while jumping to a solution.

questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the same rail operator's EA team, now working the Business Architecture. The operator uses the TOGAF Standard and the CIO sponsors the program. Key stakeholders have agreed at a high level on the integration work, and a Baseline Business Architecture exists (a business capability map and value stream descriptions for the national network). The Board has set a 12-month first phase to unify timetabling across the merged network. A packaged timetabling suite is on the table but aligns poorly with the operator's current planning processes.
questions.q: The team leader asks how you would identify the required changes in the Business Architecture. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You determine where the business (organizational design, planning processes, and so on) does not support unified timetabling, identifying what must change and the work needed. You describe the options and their costs to stakeholders so they can decide, identify where trade-offs are needed, and work with stakeholders to resolve them.
o.B: You review and update the current architecture descriptions, draw up target descriptions with new value streams and a capability map for the merged timetabling business, map value stream stages to capabilities, and run a capability gap analysis to show what must change.
o.C: You model the current state using capabilities, value streams, organization mapping, and information mapping, focus on improving capabilities and value streams because baselines already exist, and document where the business must change.
o.D: You request detailed documentation for the packaged timetabling suite, define the changes needed to align it with existing planning processes, sequence them in an Architecture Roadmap, and obtain customer references to confirm the vendor can meet the 12-month date and SLAs.

rat.A: Best (5). Phase B is about the business: find where it does not support the change, describe options and costs, and work with stakeholders on trade-offs so they make informed decisions.
rat.B: Second (3). Updating descriptions and drafting a target with a capability gap analysis is a valid technique to find change, but it is more model-focused, and at this stage you need not commit to a packaged solution.
rat.C: Third (1). Modeling only, with no stakeholder engagement, and it wrongly assumes the focus is capabilities and value streams just because baselines exist.
rat.D: Distractor (0). This is not Business Architecture; it is implicit architecture with the architect acting as stakeholder, SME, and implementer, jumping straight to a vendor solution.

questions.stitle: Scenario 3 - Rail operator, passenger information data
questions.scenario: You are a Senior Architect in the rail operator's EA team responsible for the passenger-information Application and Data Architecture. The operator uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the program. A review of the Business Architecture with key stakeholders found that fragmented data across the two networks produces inconsistent real-time passenger information and drives up the cost of running duplicate feeds. Stakeholders agree the passenger experience can improve, but the current information flows consume large IT resources. The team leader wants to address the stated motivation to drive down sustained cost.
questions.q: The team leader asks what you need to know to address the motivation to drive down sustained costs. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You identify where the Application Architecture (information system services and logical application components) fails to support consistent passenger information and drives cost up, determine the changes to information flows that improve the experience and drive down sustained cost, and identify stakeholder priorities for the enhanced capability, value stream, and information flow.
o.B: You produce current-state application and data models, develop a Target Architecture model showing how to improve passenger information and reduce cost, create views describing the changes, and identify gaps between current and target to define roadmap components.
o.C: You determine where the Application and Data Architecture create the information-flow problem, identify the changes needed to fix it, look for incremental changes that improve the passenger experience, identify the one-time work and impact to reduce sustainment cost, then check with stakeholders whether the experience improvements are worth the one-time and ongoing cost.
o.D: You determine where the Application and Data Architecture fail to support consistent passenger information and drive cost up, focus on the logical application and logical data components, identify the changes and the work required, and obtain stakeholder priorities on the application development, data structures, and interfaces.

rat.A: Second (3). It identifies stakeholder priorities and changes to information flows, but does not explicitly assess the one-time and ongoing costs of the change with stakeholders. This leaves cost-of-change information needed by Phases E and F incomplete.
rat.B: Distractor (0). Jumps straight to modeling and optimizing the Application and Data Architecture with no linkage to the value-stream and information-flow deficiencies identified in the Business Architecture.
rat.C: Best (5). Every change carries value and cost, and stakeholders accept a Target Architecture on the cost of change and expected outcome, not on a data model. You discover where the current Application and Data Architecture cause the deficiency, then assess the direct and sustainment cost of the change with stakeholders, feeding Phase E and Phase F.
rat.D: Third (1). It identifies logical components but does not analyze the information flows known to cause the deficiency, produces no actual target for change, and asks stakeholders for priorities on implementation details.

questions.stitle: Scenario 4 - Rail operator, trackside network refresh
questions.scenario: You are the Technology Architect in the rail operator's EA team. The operator uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the program. The Business, Data, and Application Architectures for the integrated passenger-information system have been developed and agreed with key stakeholders. The trackside communications network inherited from the franchise uses ageing hardware that cannot meet the availability and latency the target applications require. Stakeholders have raised cost and operational-continuity concerns about any technology change. You must determine the required changes in the Technology Architecture.
questions.q: You have been asked how you would identify the required changes in the Technology Architecture. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You select a modern trackside network platform from a preferred vendor that meets availability and latency, define the migration steps to install it, and present the implementation schedule to stakeholders for approval.
o.B: You determine where the current technology platform does not support the target applications' availability and latency needs, identify the technology gaps and the work to close them, describe the options and their cost, effort, and risk to stakeholders, and work with them on the trade-offs so they can decide.
o.C: You build a baseline Technology Portfolio Catalog and a target platform decomposition, run a technology gap analysis against the target applications, and document candidate roadmap components for the gaps.
o.D: You catalog the current trackside technology, note which components are non-standard, and hand the list to the infrastructure team to plan replacements while you move on to Phase E.

rat.A: Distractor (0). This jumps to a specific vendor solution and an implementation schedule, acting as SME and implementer rather than developing the Technology Architecture and letting stakeholders weigh options.
rat.B: Best (5). Phase D determines where the technology does not support the target, identifies the gaps and work, and presents options with cost, effort, and risk so stakeholders can make the trade-off decision that addresses their continuity and cost concerns.
rat.C: Second (3). Baseline and target catalogs plus a gap analysis are valid Phase D techniques that surface candidate roadmap components, but this is model-focused and does not engage stakeholders on the cost and risk trade-offs they raised.
rat.D: Third (1). Cataloging and flagging non-standard components is partial Phase D work, but delegating the change decision to the infrastructure team skips the target definition, options, and stakeholder trade-offs.

questions.stitle: Scenario 5 - Rail operator, staged rollout to a deliverable plan
questions.scenario: You are an Enterprise Architect at the rail operator. It uses the TOGAF Standard and the CIO sponsors the program. An Architecture Vision and a set of domain architectures with identified gaps have been approved for the ticketing and passenger-information integration. Stakeholders have stressed that the live network cannot tolerate a big-bang cutover and that each step must deliver measurable value to passengers. The Governing Board wants risk controlled and value delivered progressively.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend how to move from the approved gaps to a deliverable plan. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You direct each domain architect to produce projects that close their domain's gaps, then sum the work into the Implementation and Migration Plan and record the timeline in the Architecture Roadmap.
o.B: You ask stakeholders to state what must be done to implement the domain architectures, roll the result into an IT portfolio plan, and produce a comprehensive Target Architecture with detailed technology choices for the next five years.
o.C: You identify dependencies among the changes and organize them into work packages addressing the gaps, assess the value, effort, and risk of each change and work package against stakeholder priorities, define a series of Transition Architectures that each deliver measurable business value, and document the work packages and Transition Architectures in the Architecture Roadmap.
o.D: You implement the domain architectures immediately, revise all in-flight projects to align, expose all data and functionality through service interfaces, and publish the result as the Implementation and Migration Plan.

rat.A: Second (3). It addresses the deliverables but as an uncoordinated, domain-by-domain roll-up, does not use Transition Architectures for incremental value, though it names the roadmap and plan correctly.
rat.B: Third (1). It considers stakeholder input but ends in fixed five-year technology choices, negating incremental value and the ability to absorb change.
rat.C: Best (5). This is the Phase E approach: dependencies to work packages, value/effort/risk against stakeholder priorities, Transition Architectures delivering incremental value, documented in the Architecture Roadmap, directly serving the no-big-bang, progressive-value concern.
rat.D: Distractor (0). It jumps to a technical solution, ignores transition and value, and does not follow Phase E guidance.

questions.stitle: Scenario 6 - Rail operator, detailed migration plan
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at the rail operator, which uses the TOGAF ADM; the CIO sponsors the program. An outline Implementation and Migration Plan is approved and detailed planning is underway. Others outside the EA team will fund, build, support, and operate the result, and the regional operations lines have resisted new operating models. The CIO wants risk reduction, an incremental rollout, and key value delivered with each increment.
questions.q: You have been asked how the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan should be created. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Business Planning, Portfolio Management, and Operations Management join the EA team in migration planning; you create detailed resource estimates and business value for all deliverables, plan a series of Transition Architectures considering stakeholder priorities, then finalize the plan and complete the architecture development cycle.
o.B: The EA team's domain architects define Transition Architectures to deliver value incrementally, create a prioritized activity list documented in the plan with a detailed schedule in the roadmap, and circulate these to the lines of business and Executive Board so they are ready to fund the work.
o.C: You finalize the plan with the domain architects and submit it to the Architecture Board for approval, incorporating feedback; the plan includes a prioritized project list, approximate cost, effort, schedule, and a sequenced timeline used as the roadmap.
o.D: Project Managers use the Phase E Implementation and Migration Strategy to build project plans on scope, budget, and time, define business value per project, select the highest-value projects, and request funding from the Architecture Board.

rat.A: Best (5). Phase F emphasizes collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization (Business Planning, Portfolio, Operations), resource estimates and business value for deliverables, and Transition Architectures based on stakeholder priorities.
rat.B: Second (3). It uses Transition Architectures but is EA-team-centric and lacks the close collaborative planning across the wider stakeholder groups.
rat.C: Third (1). Incomplete; it misses the collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization.
rat.D: Distractor (0). This hands strategic migration planning to Project Managers, whereas TOGAF's intent is that the EA gives projects detailed guidance so they focus on operational, not strategic, issues.

questions.stitle: Scenario 7 - Rail operator, non-standard control gateway
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at the rail operator, which has a mature EA capability using the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the program. After consulting key stakeholders, the CIO has decided to deploy a COTS real-time information package quickly and within budget. The package needs a signalling-network gateway that is not on the current infrastructure standards list. The Architecture Board noted the non-standard component and the need to protect availability and safety KPIs. The CIO has approved the roadmap projects and appointed a project manager.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend a plan to implement the CIO's direction. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You ask the vendor to modify the gateway to meet current standards, build a prototype to explore options, obtain internal development leads' approval, then hand a schedule-focused project plan to the project manager and review performance after go-live.
o.B: You accept the direction, add the gateway as an additional organizational standard in the Standards Library (noting the training and skills needed to support it), work with the implementation team to draw up an Architecture Contract, emphasize compliance reviews and availability and safety testing during implementation, agree SLAs and dates with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
o.C: You eliminate the non-standard gateway, create a plan and Architecture Contract to build a standards-compliant replacement in-house, tell the CIO this is cheaper long-term, take the budget impact to the finance committee, and chair frequent project meetings to monitor compliance.
o.D: You prepare a risk assessment and impact analysis of the non-standard gateway, hand deliverables and dates to the implementation team, obtain CIO approval, test the solution just before deployment, and archive artifacts in the repository when done.

rat.A: Second (3). Vendor change and a prototype cost the time and budget the scenario forbids, the project plan is the PM's job rather than the architect's, and testing performance only after go-live is too late.
rat.B: Best (5). All within Phase G: accept the stakeholder-informed decision, add the new standard to the Standards Library, form an Architecture Contract with the implementation team, run compliance reviews and testing during implementation, agree SLAs with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
rat.C: Distractor (0). It reverses a decision the CIO already made with stakeholders, makes unsubstantiated cost claims, and has the architect chairing PM meetings.
rat.D: Third (1). It follows the direction but focuses on risk over co-existence, just hands over schedules, and tests too late, after the solution is built.

questions.stitle: Scenario 8 - Rail operator, post-deployment change request
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at the rail operator. The integrated passenger-information architecture has been deployed and is under Architecture Change Management. The operator uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the program. A national accessibility regulation has just been enacted requiring new real-time audio information across all stations. The operations director has raised a Change Request describing the new requirement. Stakeholders want to know whether this is a routine update to the current architecture or something larger.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend how to handle the Change Request. Which is the best answer?

o.A: You treat the regulation as a routine maintenance change, direct the operations team to add the audio feature to the deployed system, and record the update in the repository.
o.B: You assess the Change Request in the change management process, evaluate its impact on the current architecture, requirements, and business value, classify whether it can be met by a change to the existing architecture or requires a new ADM cycle, and make a recommendation to the stakeholders who decide.
o.C: You immediately initiate a full new ADM cycle from the Architecture Vision to redesign the passenger-information architecture around the accessibility regulation.
o.D: You log the Change Request, prepare a requirements impact assessment noting the affected requirements and stakeholder priority, and reference it in the repository so it can be considered at the next architecture review.

rat.A: Distractor (0). Assuming it is routine and pushing it straight to operations skips the impact assessment and the decision about whether a new ADM cycle is warranted, and it takes a decision that belongs to stakeholders.
rat.B: Best (5). Phase H assesses the Change Request, evaluates impact on architecture, requirements, and value, and determines whether a change to the existing architecture suffices or a new ADM cycle is needed, with stakeholders deciding.
rat.C: Third (1). Jumping to a full new ADM cycle before assessing impact over-reacts; Phase H first decides whether a lighter change would suffice.
rat.D: Second (3). Logging the request and a requirements impact assessment are correct inputs, but this defers the classification and recommendation about a new cycle rather than completing the Phase H assessment now.
